a7v: Germany's own tank, of which only twenty were built, first went into action in March 1918. At Villers-Bretonneux one met British tanks in the first tank battle.
albatros-d-iii: A sleek German fighter with two synchronised machine guns and a narrow lower wing. It ruled the sky over Arras in the Bloody April of 1917.
anti-tank: A light, low gun that stops armoured vehicles with direct fire. Purpose-built anti-tank guns appeared only in 1918; before that, field guns did the job.
armored-car: A machine-gun car on a motor chassis, plated against rifle fire. Fast on roads but bound to them, it is at its best in a war of movement.
armored-train: A locomotive with armoured wagons carrying guns and machine guns. It defends and raids along the railway, but can never leave the track.
battleship: The heaviest warship of the fleet, armed with big guns in turrets. The British and German dreadnought fleets met in full only once, at Jutland in 1916.
bunker: A concrete strongpoint built to hold a sector of the front. Its thick walls shrug off light fire, but it cannot move.
cavalry: Mounted troops for scouting, screening and pursuit. Vital in the open fighting of 1914, they lost much of their role once trenches and machine guns froze the front.
charron: Charron built one of the first armoured cars with a turret before the war. This French car carries a machine gun and scouts fast along the roads.
construction-unit: Engineers and labourers who build roads, bridges, railways and field works. Their work keeps the army supplied and moving behind the front.
destroyer: A fast, lightly armoured warship built to hunt torpedo boats and later submarines. Destroyers screen the battle fleets and escort convoys.
dh2: A British single-seat pusher, its engine behind the pilot so the Lewis gun fires freely ahead. It helped end the Fokker Scourge in 1916.
dh4: A fast British two-seat day bomber of 1917, able to outrun many fighters. America built it in large numbers too, with the Liberty engine.
elite-infantry: Picked assault troops trained to fight with grenades and light machine guns. They infiltrate weak points and overrun positions that line infantry cannot take.
fokker-d-vii: Germany's best fighter of 1918, easy to fly and strong at altitude. The Armistice terms named it explicitly among the aircraft to be handed over.
fokker-dr-i: Fokker's triplane climbs and turns better than almost anything in the air. Manfred von Richthofen flew one in red and was killed in it in April 1918.
fokker-e-i: The first fighter with a machine gun synchronised to fire through the propeller. From mid-1915 it gave German pilots the upper hand: the Fokker Scourge.
fokker-e-iii: The most numerous of Fokker's monoplane fighters, firing through the propeller like the E.I. It ruled the front until the D.H.2 and Nieuport 11 arrived in 1916.
gotha-g-vb: A twin-engined German heavy bomber that flies mostly by night. Gothas bombed London and southern England in 1917 and 1918.
handley-page-0400: A large British twin-engined night bomber with folding wings for storage. In 1918 it raided railways and industry in western Germany.
heavy-artillery: Large-calibre howitzers and siege guns that hurl heavy shells deep behind the enemy line. Slow to move, they smashed fortresses in 1914 and trenches thereafter.
infantry: Riflemen who hold and take ground, the backbone of every army. They dig in, wait out bombardments and advance across no man's land.
junkers-j4: An armoured German two-seater, built almost entirely of metal, for low-level work over the trenches. Its steel shell protects crew and engine from ground fire.
light-artillery: Quick-firing field guns drawn by horses, such as the French 75 mm and the German 77 mm. They keep up with the troops and fire fast.
mark-i: The first tank ever to go into battle, at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916. Its rhomboid tracks run all round the hull to cross wide trenches.
mark-iv: The most numerous British tank, armoured against the German armour-piercing bullet. It led the massed attack at Cambrai in 1917; Germany used captured ones.
medium-artillery: Medium howitzers and long guns, heavier than field guns yet still mobile. They reach enemy batteries and strongpoints behind the front line.
mobile-aa: An anti-aircraft gun on a lorry that moves with the front to cover troops and roads. Both sides fielded such motor guns, the French using their 75 mm.
morane-saulnier-n: A small French monoplane fighter with steel wedges on its propeller to deflect its own bullets. Few were built, but the British also flew it from 1916.
nieuport-xvii: A nimble French sesquiplane fighter of 1916 with a gun firing over or through the propeller. Aces such as Nungesser, Albert Ball and Billy Bishop flew it.
patrol-boat: A small armed boat for rivers, coasts and harbours. It guards the waterways with a light gun and watches for enemy movement.
renault-ft17: The first tank with its gun in a fully rotating turret, the layout of nearly every later tank. Light and cheap, it was built in thousands in 1918.
sappers: Combat engineers who dig trenches, saps and mines and clear obstacles. They break into fortifications and open passages under fire.
se5a: A fast, robust British fighter of 1917 and a steady gun platform with Vickers and Lewis guns. James McCudden and Edward Mannock flew it.
sopwith-camel: Named for the hump over its twin Vickers guns, the Camel is tricky to fly but turns sharply. It downed more enemy aircraft than any other Allied fighter.
spad-vii: A sturdy French fighter of 1916 with a Hispano-Suiza engine, fast and strong in a dive. Georges Guynemer flew it with the Storks squadron.
spad-xiii: The twin-gun successor of the SPAD VII, fast and rugged. French and American squadrons flew it in 1918, among them Eddie Rickenbacker.
st-chamond: A French tank whose long hull overhangs its tracks, with a 75 mm gun in the nose. Its petrol-electric drive was advanced, but it ditched easily in trenches.
static-aa: A fixed anti-aircraft battery guarding a town, depot or bridge. Its gunners fire time-fused shells that burst near the aircraft rather than hit it.
static-balloon: A tethered kite balloon that lifts observers high above the lines. They direct artillery fire by telephone and jump by parachute when attacked.
submarine: A submarine strikes ships with torpedoes, unseen beneath the surface. German U-boat campaigns threatened Britain's supply until convoys checked them in 1917.
supply-car: A motor lorry that brings ammunition, fuel and rations up to the troops. In 1916 endless lorry columns kept Verdun supplied along a single road.
torpedo-boat: A small, fast warship that strikes larger ships with torpedoes. It relies on speed and darkness rather than armour.
train-artillery: A heavy gun on a railway mounting, far too big for any road carriage. It fires from the rails at targets deep behind the front.
transport-ship: A merchant ship carrying troops and supplies across the sea. Unarmed and slow, it needs warships to protect it.
transport-train: A supply train that brings ammunition and stores up to the railheads. Railways carry the war's material, and whole armies depend on them.
voisin-iii: A French steel-framed pusher biplane and day bomber. On 5 October 1914 one shot down a German Aviatik, the first air victory by gunfire.
zeppelin-staaken-r-vi: One of the German giant bombers, with four engines and a crew of seven. From 1917 they bombed London by night, some dropping 1,000 kg bombs.
